pages.text:
The cart stopped with its front wheel in the gate's drainage groove.

For a moment Senn Arlow kept pulling. Their boots scraped on the stones. The two people seated beneath the cart's canvas cover leaned forward with them, as if the extra effort might persuade the wheel.

It did not.

“Don't pull harder,” Tamsin said through the bars.

Senn looked up. “I had reached that conclusion.”

“The brake's caught under the rim.”

“I know where it is. I can't reach it while I hold this.”

The gate shuddered. Senn put a shoulder against the nearer leaf, keeping a gap no wider than their arm. On the far side of the passage, a wheel turned through a quarter circle and stopped. Something behind it dragged metal over stone.

Mara set down her rifle before she approached the bars.

“How many with you?”

“Two on the cart. Two who can walk. One who says he can.”

“I can,” said the man nearest the opening.

“Then you can help me by sitting down,” Senn replied.

The man remained standing. He had a folded coat under one arm and no shoes. Iona looked at his feet, then caught herself and looked at his face.

“Would you let me have a look?”

“At which part?”

“The part you would like me to start with.”

He considered her. “Left heel. The right one still belongs to me.”

Iona knelt outside the opening. He passed his foot through as carefully as if he were lending her something expensive.

Behind Mara, Renn Tallow lowered the square signal board they had been carrying.

Iven Cair had been trying a quiet rhythm on the side of his concertina. At the third tap, the man without shoes lifted his head.

“Could you leave that?”

Iven stopped. “Sorry. Thought it might help.”

“It sounds like they’re coming down the stairs.”

“Right.” He shifted his fingers off the wood. “I’ll ask next time.”

Mara knew him from the hall, where he had moved scenery for years. He had only recently entered the Bard discipline. The repaired concertina was his; deciding when to use it was work he had barely begun.

“Six people?” Renn asked.

“Including the one holding your gate,” said Senn.

Renn examined the board. A strip of paper had been pinned across its bottom edge. The paper was dry beneath the overhang, though the rest of the board bore streaks of rain.

Mara knew the form. She had used it often enough to recognize the space where a runner signed a completed delivery.

“What time did that arrive?” she asked.

“Before first light.”

“From where?”

“Inside.”

“Which office?”

Renn turned the board toward her. The strip bore two stamps and a heavy line of type: EVACUATION COMPLETE. There was no runner's signature.

“I asked that too,” Renn said.

Mara read it again, looking for a detail that would make the instruction belong to someone. The stamps were clean. The corner reserved for a name was blank.

“Then take it off the board.”

“And put what in its place?”

She almost said that it did not matter. Six people were waiting at the gate. That was enough to make the instruction wrong.

It was not enough to tell the next cart where to go.

“How many are on your road?” she asked.

Renn looked past her, toward the bend beyond the watch shelter. “Nine at the last count. More coming from the water steps.”

“Walking in?”

“They heard there was transport out.”

Senn laughed once, without amusement. “So did we.”

The wheel on the far side began to turn again.

Bram stepped into the gap beside Senn and planted his shield against the gate. The pressure took him by surprise. His boots shifted back half a pace before he found a brace against the stonework.

“You can let go,” he told Senn.

Senn did, slowly. The relief in their face disappeared when they saw Bram's shoulders settle under the weight.

“How long can you hold it?”

“Long enough to look at the wheel.”

“That wasn't the question.”

“No,” he said. “It wasn't.”

Hux crouched beside Tamsin. Through the bars, she guided his hand under the cart's brake arm.

“Up a little. Toward you. Stop.”

The arm sprang free with a crack. Hux withdrew his hand and looked at the line of rust across his palm.

“It needs a washer.”

“It needs a new brake,” Tamsin said.

“We have neither,” Senn told them.

Hux felt through his coat pockets. He found a button, a piece of wire, and a flattened metal cap. He laid the button aside.

“For the moment,” he said, “we have this.”

“Will it hold on a slope?”

“Not by itself.”

“Then I need someone at the back.”

“You have me.”

Senn nodded. Only then did they take their hands off the cart.

Vale had moved to the inner edge of the watch shelter, where chalk names crowded the wall. Some were full names. Others were descriptions. A woman in a green shawl. A boy with a dog. At shoulder height, someone had marked a date beside two short lines.

Dara Flint moved out of Hux’s way and caught the end of her scabbard in a broken paving joint. She took another step before she understood why it would not follow.

“Checking the stones?” Hux asked.

“Yes.”

He looked down.

“No,” she said. “Give me a moment.”

She kept the drawn sword pointed away from him while he lifted the scabbard clear. Tamsin glanced at the strap.

“That sits low. Want me to shorten it?”

“After this.” Dara looked at the gate, where Bram was still braced. “Please.”

Mara had brought tools to Dara’s grinding bench before either of them had entered their present disciplines. Dara had known what to do with those. The sword training was recent, and apparently there was more to carrying one than having sharpened it.

Joss Merrow leaned around Hux to catch Senn's eye.

“The ward behind the dyers' bridge?”

“Uphill side.”

“My uncle calls that the new yard.”

“So does everyone who hasn't been there lately.”

Joss took a scrap of wrapping paper from his satchel. There were three addresses on it, each with a small square beside it. He added the turn Senn had given him without crossing out any of the others.

“You still doing deliveries?” Senn asked.

“Trying to finish them.”

The wooden caller baton knocked against his buckle as he put the paper away. He caught it before it struck again. He had entered Summoner training recently; before that, people in the market had known him by the parcels he arrived with. Some still did.

“After we open this,” Senn said.

Joss nodded and moved back so Hux had room to work.

Vale took a folded sheet from their coat.

“Did you write these?” they asked Senn.

“Some.”

“May I copy them?”

Senn glanced toward Renn. “For the watch?”

“For the people looking for them.”

“Those aren't always different people.”

Vale lowered the sheet.

“All right. Tell me which ones I can take.”

Senn studied them for a moment, then pointed to three names near the bottom. “Those. Their families are waiting by the water steps. Leave the descriptions for now. I don't know who wrote them.”

Renn set the signal board against the wall.

“If they're waiting there, I can send someone.”

“You can tell them where we are going,” Senn said. “Once someone tells me.”

Iona finished wrapping the man's heel. “The old customs shed has a roof. We brought blankets. There is room for six to lie down.”

“And water?”

“Two covered jars.”

“A place to leave the cart?”

“Beside the door.”

“It comes back with me.”

Iona looked up. “You aren't coming out with them?”

“There are people at the next passage who still need it.”

“How many?”

“I haven't reached them.”

She glanced at the worn canvas cover, the improvised brake and the wheel still sitting in the drainage groove. “We could carry the people who can walk and give you a rest.”

Senn shook their head. “Help me make a trip I can repeat.”

Mara turned to Renn. “Will you keep the road open to the shed?”

“For these six.”

“For anyone who comes through.”

“If you bring fifty, that roof won't get larger.”

Mara felt the old impatience rise: the need to settle the terms, assign the work and have everyone move. Renn had always been good at finding the difficulty that came after an instruction.

Usually because someone would have to stand in it.

“Keep a count,” she said. “When the shed is full, send word. We find the next place before we bring the next cart.”

“And the people already on my road?”

“Tell them exactly what we have. Don't promise transport we haven't seen.”

Renn took the paper from the signal board. The pin caught, tearing one corner. They folded it around the pin rather than dropping either into the gutter.

“I want this back,” they said, holding it toward Mara.

“The board?”

“The answer. When you find out who sent it.”

Mara put the folded instruction in her coat. “I'll bring you what I find.”

A bell sounded beyond the gate.

Bram's shield struck the stone jamb. He bent one knee and caught the next movement before it could close the gap.

Sable had been watching the far wheel.

“It moved at the second stroke,” she said.

Tamsin looked through the bars. “Could be a release on the bell wire.”

“Or someone pulling when they hear it.”

“Can you tell?”

“Not from here.”

Mara leaned close enough to see past the cart. A watch captain stood at the wheel. His sleeve had split at the elbow. One hand worked the lever while the other remained fixed around the spoke, dragging with it when it turned.

He wore the same pattern of coat she had worn.

“Captain,” she called.

The wheel stopped.

For a moment she could hear the people beneath the canvas breathing. Then the captain lifted his head. His mouth moved, but the bell sounded over it.

The lever came down.

“Again,” Bram said through his teeth. “If you're going to talk to him, do it again.”

Mara reached for her rifle. She did not raise it yet.

“Captain. There are six people at your gate.”

The captain's free hand opened. Its fingers made a small, precise movement above the lever, as if searching for a missing handle.

Then it closed again.

Tamsin followed his hand with her eyes. “That lever has to stay up before the cart can pass.”

“Can we reach it?” Mara asked.

“From his side.”

Hux kept one hand on the freed brake arm. Iona withdrew the man's foot from the opening and asked him to keep the bandage dry. Vale tucked the three permitted names inside the folded sheet.

Senn put a hand on Bram's shoulder.

“When you can open it, say so before you move. I have to lift the wheel out of that groove.”

Bram nodded. “I'll say.”

Mara looked once at Renn. The runner had turned the board over and was marking the road to the shed on its clean back.

She passed through the gap.

The wheel had stopped. The gate was still shut.

For several breaths nobody moved toward it. A loose end of wire tapped the watch captain's sleeve. When the wind turned, it tapped again.

“Bram?” Senn called from the other side.

“Here.”

“Can I move the cart?”

Tamsin crouched beside the lever. The captain's hand lay across its base. She shifted the hand clear with the folded edge of his coat, then looked into the slot beneath it.

“Not yet. There's a tooth caught in the return.”

She held out her palm. Hux gave her the flattened cap.

“I was using that,” he said.

“You'll get it back bent.”

“That would be an improvement.”

He went to the gate before she could answer. On the other side, Senn had both hands on the cart again.

Mara watched Tamsin work. The captain's cuff had ridden up when she moved his hand. A pale line crossed his wrist beneath the grime, where a watch strap had once kept the weather off.

She had the same line.

“Did you know him?” she asked Senn.

“Enough to ask him to open this yesterday.”

Mara waited.

“He wanted an admission stamp for the cart. I told him I was taking people out, not bringing them in.”

“What did he say?”

“He asked for it again.”

The answer was so ordinary that Mara looked back at the lever. It was easier to look at a mechanism that had gone wrong.

“Watch freight passed through,” Senn added. “I saw the sacks. Don't write down that the gate wouldn't open.”

Vale, who had taken out their sheet, stopped with the pencil above it.

“May I keep that account?”

“That part. Ask before you add where I was going.”

They drew a short line under the three copied names and began a separate paragraph.

The tooth came free with a noise like a dropped spoon. Tamsin stood and pulled the lever upward. The wheel moved a little, then caught.

“Bram, take the weight. Hux, when the leaf opens, hold it there. Don't let it run.”

Bram eased his shield away from the jamb. Hux caught the gate with both hands. For a moment the opening narrowed; then the wheel completed its turn and daylight reached the groove where the cart had stuck.

“Now,” Bram said. “Lift your wheel.”

Senn lifted. The barefoot man stooped beside them despite Iona's warning and put his shoulder under the cart rail. They raised it together. The wheel cleared the stone with an ugly scraping sound.

“That heel will need looking at again,” Iona said.

“It was attached to the rest of me,” he replied. “The rest had a job.”

“So did the bandage.”

He glanced down. A red spot was spreading through it.

“Then we can both apologize at the shed.”

Iona took the folded coat from under his arm. He let her. She put it over his shoulders before taking his elbow.

The two walkers followed: a woman carrying an empty birdcage and a boy with a bundle tied in a flour sack. When the boy reached the threshold, he stepped back to let the woman pass first. She caught his sleeve and brought him alongside her.

Hux moved to the rear of the cart as promised. Senn tested the brake before trusting him with the slope. The repaired arm held for one turn of the wheel, slipped, and caught again.

“You said it wouldn't hold by itself.”

“Still true.”

“Good. I can work with true.”

They took the cart down the short incline. The woman under the left side of the canvas pushed the cover back. A square of embroidery sat in her lap, its needle fixed through the cloth.

“My box is under the seat,” she told Hux. “If you tip us, catch that first.”

“And you?”

“I can shout.”

The other passenger made a small sound. Hux thought it was a cough until the woman began to laugh with him.

Renn came up from the bend with two people carrying a door between them. They had taken its handle off so it would lie flat. Mara stepped aside to let them through.

“For the shed,” Renn said. “We can put it over the crates. Keeps a blanket off the wet floor.”

“Who gave it to you?”

“The woman whose roof you volunteered.”

Mara looked toward the customs building.

“She wants someone to fetch her husband from the water steps,” Renn continued. “She'll come tell you which one. Please let her finish the description.”

“I will.”

Renn watched her for another moment, then helped carry the door onward.

Sable remained beside the wheel. There was a brass plate below it, partly hidden by the captain's coat. She pulled the coat clear without turning the body over.

EVACUATION COMPLETE.

The letters were filled with black enamel. There were two screw holes above them and two below. At the lower right, a fresh burr marked where a tool had slipped.

Mara took the folded instruction from her pocket. The same words, the same clean stamps. Paper outside; brass inside.

“A copy?” she asked.

“At least two objects saying the same thing,” Sable said. “I haven't earned the rest yet.”

She touched neither the plate nor the wire.

“And the bell?”

“The wheel stopped. The bell hasn't. That gives us something to test.”

Beyond the passage, a note sounded over the roofs. Mara counted its strokes. This time the lever stayed where Tamsin had left it.

Tamsin put the bent cap into her hand.

“For Hux. Tell him I owe him another.”

“What keeps the gate open now?”

“This wedge until the next person takes it out. I'll mark it. Then someone has to look at it when they pass. There isn't a repair that replaces that.”

She took a piece of yellow chalk from her pocket and marked the wedge and the stone above it with matching bars.

Bram glanced at the captain. “He's in the return path.”

Mara knelt and folded the coat across his chest. Together they moved him into the watch shelter, clear of the threshold. She checked his pockets for an identification card and found a damp tobacco pouch, a key and a folded blank form. The key stayed on the bench beside him. Vale recorded where they had put it.

The captain had asked twice for a stamp he had not required of freight. He had also carried a blank form in his pocket. Neither fact explained the other.

Mara left them both in the account.

At the shed, the barefoot man had been given a crate to sit on. The woman with the embroidery was telling a stranger how to fit a blanket around the door's exposed hinge.

“Evi Pell,” she said when Iona asked her name. “This is Jorren Saye. He'd tell you himself if you stopped asking him whether he can speak.”

Jorren lifted two fingers from the blanket in greeting.

Iona nodded to him. “Would you prefer questions you can answer that way?”

He lifted one finger.

“One for yes?”

One finger again.

Evi returned to the blanket. Iona waited for Jorren's answer before moving it.

Senn had backed the empty cart against the shed wall. Hux was trying the brake while they watched. The first jar of water was already below its shoulder.

“We need a wheel chock,” Senn said. “And something to cover that wire. It will cut the next hand.”

Hux looked around the yard. A short piece of firewood lay under the customs step. He asked the shed owner before taking it.

Renn turned the signal board toward Mara. Five marks occupied the space beneath SHED. Below them were the words: ONE PLACE LEFT. ASK HERE BEFORE NEXT CART.

“You didn't count Senn,” Mara said.

“Senn told me they're going back.”

Mara looked at the porter. They were wrapping the brake wire with a strip of discarded canvas.

“Do you want an escort?”

“To the next passage. After that I know the ward. I'll bring the cart back here if the road stays usable.”

“It will,” Mara began.

Renn's pencil stopped.

“We'll check it,” Mara said. “And send word if it changes.”

Renn finished the mark they had been making.

Senn drew three short routes on the back of a customs form. One reached the triage passage, where people were waiting. One went under the registry arch, where the names on the wall could be checked against the missing lists. The third passed the workshop wire that still carried the bell's instruction deeper into the cordon.

“I can show you the turn for each,” they said. “I can't take the cart down all three.”

Vale folded their account with the copied names facing inward. Mara kept the paper instruction in a separate pocket. Hux brought the cart forward and tested the covered brake once more.

Mara went back to Renn before following them.

“I haven't found who sent it.”

“I can see that.”

“There is a brass copy inside. Same wording. I left it where it was.”
Renn wrote that beneath the question on the board. There was room for an answer, when they had one.
